content: A considerable number of patients initiating dialysis require the placement of either temporary or tunnelled haemodialysis catheters. These catheters can be inserted using two primary techniques: the traditional blind method based on anatomical landmarks or with the assistance of real-time ultrasound guidance. It has been proposed that employing ultrasound guidance during catheter placement may reduce immediate complications, such as pneumothorax or accidental arterial puncture. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effectiveness of real-time two-dimensional (2-D) Doppler ultrasound guidance compared to the traditional anatomical landmark method for the insertion of percutaneous central venous catheters in dialysis patients. Specifically, the review aimed to assess outcomes such as success rates, complications, and procedural efficiency. To gather relevant data, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Renal Group's Specialised Register, MEDLINE, EMBASE, and the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL). Reference lists of identified studies and narrative reviews were also screened. The search was last updated in January 2011. The review included all randomised controlled trials (RCTs) and quasi-RCTs that compared ultrasound-guided catheter insertion to the traditional landmark method. Both cuffed and uncuffed central venous catheters were considered. Two authors independently assessed the risk of bias in the included studies and extracted data. Statistical analyses were performed using a random-effects model, with results expressed as risk ratios (RR) for binary outcomes and mean differences (MD) for continuous outcomes, along with 95% confidence intervals (CI). Seven studies involving 767 patients and 830 catheter insertions were included in the analysis. Among these studies, three described the method of random sequence generation, but none provided details on allocation concealment. Blinding of participants and personnel was not feasible due to the nature of the intervention. The findings demonstrated that real-time ultrasound guidance significantly reduced the risk of catheter placement failure on the first attempt (5 studies, 595 catheters; RR 0.40, 95% CI 0.30 to 0.52). Additionally, the risk of arterial puncture was markedly lower with ultrasound guidance (6 studies, 535 catheters; RR 0.13, 95% CI 0.04 to 0.37), as was the risk of haematoma formation (4 studies, 323 catheters; RR 0.22, 95% CI 0.06 to 0.81). The use of ultrasound also reduced the time required for successful cannulation (1 study, 73 catheters; MD -1.40 minutes, 95% CI -2.17 to -0.63) and decreased the number of attempts needed per catheter insertion (1 study, 110 catheters; MD -0.35, 95% CI -0.54 to -0.16). In conclusion, the use of real-time 2-D Doppler ultrasound guidance offers significant advantages over the traditional landmark method for haemodialysis catheter placement. These benefits include higher success rates on the first attempt, reduced risk of arterial puncture and haematomas, shorter procedural times, and fewer insertion attempts.
